skillLevels.label: Awareness
skillLevels.description: Has little to no practical experience. Relies entirely on guidance and examples. Can perform only the most basic tasks under supervision.
skillLevels.example: Knows what a List<T> or a class is, but struggles with syntax and needs a tutorial open to write basic loops

skillLevels.label: Beginner
skillLevels.description: Understands fundamentals. Can complete simple tasks with some independence. Still needs frequent guidance for unfamiliar or complex work.
skillLevels.example: Writes standard API endpoints, uses LINQ basics, but doesn't understand underlying concepts like memory management (struct vs. class) or async/await pitfalls.

skillLevels.label: Competent
skillLevels.description: Can work independently on standard tasks. Applies best practices. Identifies issues and suggests solutions. Needs support only in complex or ambiguous cases.
skillLevels.example: Uses asynchronous programming (Task/await) correctly, understands generics, writes clean object-oriented code, and uses standard collections efficiently.

skillLevels.label: Advanced
skillLevels.description: Handles complex tasks and systems with confidence. Optimizes and improves existing solutions. Mentors others, shares knowledge, and ensures quality.
skillLevels.example: Understands high-performance memory management (Span<T>, Memory<T>), fine-tunes garbage collection impacts, and effectively debugs multi-threaded race conditions.

skillLevels.label: Expert
skillLevels.description: Recognized authority in the skill. Defines standards, anticipates risks, and sets direction. Coaches teams, drives innovation, and aligns skill application with business goals.
skillLevels.example: Writes custom source generators, contributes to open-source .NET repositories, or architects the core framework extensions used across the entire company.

topics.reasoning: The candidate has a solid, practical understanding of Onion Architecture and standard pattern implementation (such as Controller-Repository). However, they struggled with advanced domain-driven design concepts, such as defining aggregates and detailing strict dependency rules, indicating a competent developer who follows established patterns but is not yet fully designing complex structures from scratch.
topics.notes: Proposed Cart and CartItem entities for shopping cart structure. Defined the purpose of Domain, Infrastructure, and Application layers in Onion Architecture. Specified repositories (CartRepository, CartItemRepository) for data persistence. Identified common CRUD operations for repositories. Suggested a background job for cleaning up old carts. Outlined use cases for the Application layer (add/remove/update items, calculate price, clear cart). Described the API/Presentation layer with a CartController for exposing CRUD endpoints. Struggled to articulate concrete dependency rules between layers in Onion Architecture without referring to external diagrams. Provided a vague definition of DDD and how domain entities differentiate from DTOs. Justified separating the CartPriceService from the domain entity primarily for testability and separation of concerns, but did not fully address the concept of domain logic residing within the domain model itself. Did not provide a clear definition of an Aggregate in DDD or its distinction from an Entity. Initially struggled to define microservices beyond 'more than one service'. Did not initially identify independent databases as a key characteristic of microservices. Struggled to articulate how Onion Architecture aids in splitting a monolith into microservices, beyond general separation of concerns.

topics.reasoning: The candidate demonstrates practical familiarity with standard REST API design (HTTP verbs, resource nesting). However, they hit a wall regarding advanced REST principles (statelessness, uniform interface), protocol details (HTTP/2/3 features), and resolving operations that are not naturally resource-centric (like email actions), which matches the Beginner level requiring guidance on complex or non-routine API scenarios.
topics.notes: Defined POST for creation, PUT for full update, and PATCH for partial update. Explained that distinct HTTP methods provide semantic clarity for operations. Proposed a logical URL structure for shopping cart resources and nested items (e.g., /cart/{id}/items). Provided a high-level definition of REST but struggled to elaborate on its core principles (e.g., statelessness, uniform interface) and how it guarantees certain behaviors or solves specific problems (e.g., concurrency). Initially found designing a REST endpoint for 'sending email' problematic due to it being an action rather than a resource. Showed limited knowledge of HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 features (e.g., persistent connections, multiplexing), incorrectly stating REST (implicitly HTTP/1.1) does not have persistent connections. Could not explain how REST, by itself, guarantees avoidance of simultaneous data changes or ensures atomic operations.

topics.reasoning: The candidate builds with ORMs (EF Core/Dapper) and understands data storage paradigms (relational vs NoSQL document store) and core database transaction concepts (ACID). Minor gaps in explaining distributed NoSQL transaction constraints and detailed ACID elements (Isolation, Durability) align with a Competent level of solid feature delivery without deep database internals mastery.
topics.notes: Listed experience with MS SQL, PostgreSQL, SQLite, and MongoDB. Identified Entity Framework and Dapper for relational databases, and MongoDB driver for MongoDB. Clearly articulated the fundamental difference: Entity Framework for relational databases (strict schema, tables, rows, relationships) vs. MongoDB driver for document-oriented databases (flexible schema, collections, documents). Listed benefits of relational databases: strong for complex queries/joins, strict schema (predictability, error catching at DB level), data integrity (critical for financial transactions), ACID properties. Listed drawbacks of relational databases: schema changes require migrations (can be complex), slow joins on large datasets, inflexible for rapidly changing/unstructured data. Listed benefits of non-relational databases (MongoDB): flexible schema, good for horizontal scaling. Defined Atomicity (all or nothing, no intermediate state) and Consistency (valid state to valid state, no rule violation) from ACID. Struggled to articulate why transactions are inherently harder to guarantee across multiple documents/servers in distributed NoSQL compared to relational databases, though correctly linked it to horizontal scaling and consistency trade-offs. Struggled to provide a comprehensive explanation for why PostgreSQL's native JSON capabilities don't fully negate the need for a dedicated NoSQL database like MongoDB for certain use cases. Struggled with Durability from ACID. Struggled to define Isolation from ACID in his own words clearly, initially reading directly from notes.

topics.reasoning: While the candidate has practical experience using a Service Bus for event integration, they struggled with foundational messaging concepts, reliability patterns (retries, dead-letter queues), decision matrices for HTTP vs. queues, and could not name specific tech stacks (Azure Service Bus, RabbitMQ, Kafka) until guided, reflecting a Beginner level.
topics.notes: Identified HTTP requests for simple point-to-point communication. Suggested SignalR for real-time, constant connections. Provided a concrete example of using a Service Bus in a previous project for event-driven communication (updating smart lock access groups based on user role changes). Initially struggled to define Service Bus clearly, describing it generally as a 'data transferrer' or 'place for queues' rather than a message broker or platform. Did not clearly articulate the criteria for choosing different integration patterns (e.g., when to choose HTTP vs. a message queue). Struggled with how message queues ensure message delivery and prevent loss in scenarios where the consumer service crashes after receiving but before fully processing a message. Needed prompting to discuss message acknowledgment, dead-lettering, and retries. Could not name specific Service Bus technologies (e.g., RabbitMQ, Azure Service Bus, Kafka).

topics.reasoning: The candidate autonomously writes standard tests and understands the principle of isolation. They corrected an initial mistake regarding external dependencies (DateTime.Now), demonstrating solid logical troubleshooting skills.
topics.notes: Clearly defined Unit Tests: isolate a single unit of code (function, class), mock all external dependencies (DB, network), focus on logic, no real I/O. Gave an example of testing a calculator. Initially classified a date difference calculation that uses DateTime.Now as a Unit Test, then correctly identified it as having an uncontrolled external dependency, making it more akin to an Integration Test unless DateTime.Now is mocked.

topics.reasoning: The candidate accurately defined the boundary between integration and E2E testing, including browser automation. However, they did not elaborate on specific advanced test data management or complex automation setups within their own practical projects.
topics.notes: Clearly defined Integration Tests: test interaction between multiple components, use real dependencies (DB, files), minimal mocking, not fully isolated. Clearly defined End-to-End (E2E) Tests: simulate a complete user flow from UI to backend and database, highest level of testing, verifies full business processes. Provided a strong example: user opening browser, logging in, adding to cart, placing order, receiving email confirmation. Identified tools like Playwright and Selenium for E2E testing. Did not elaborate on specific strategies or tools for automated integration or E2E testing in his project.

Did not initially mention the significance of health checks or monitoring as part of the deployment process but clarified it after prompting.
